How to install linux:

  1. Download an ISO (a file that contains the operating system) for the OS you want, Solus in this case. (Although I recommend Ubuntu for new users. Ubuntu + Cinnamon Desktop will be graphically similar to windows.)

  2. Create a bootable USB drive or burn the ISO onto a disc. You'll need a program like YUMI.

  3. Boot into your Laptops BIOS (Mash F12 or F2 etc. when the laptop is booting) and select the boot order so you boot to the USB or disc instead of the hard drive.

  4. Reboot laptop, install Linux.

Google is your friend, I'm sure there's many guides out there.

1) Download Linux Mint here. Take cinnamon or mate version for Windows-like desktop (taskbar, star-menu, clock in the bottom right) or Xfce version for an OSX-type environment (taskbar at the top etc.). If you want a specific advice, go with cinnamon.

2) Burn the ISO to a DVD.

3) Put DVD in laptop, boot from DVD. If it doesn't boot from the DVD, you'll have to hit F12 or some such during the boot, get into BIOS and set the DVD first in the boot order.

4) Click the "install" shortcut you see on the desktop (if you want, you can browse around first to see how everything looks).

5) Follow the on-screen instructions. It'll ask for a user name and password, etc. At the end the computer will reboot and you're done. There will probably be some updates to install now, but basically the system is ready.

Download the ISO file for whichever distro you choose, open the applicable USB media creator, select the correct flash drive (make sure you get the right drive here! I suggest unplugging all other USB storage devices unless you are very sure you select the correct one. If you select the wrong one, you will lose all the data on it!) Select the ISO you downloaded and then hit OK, or start, or whatever the option is.

Once the program tells you it successfully created the installation media, eject the flash drive and plug it into the powered-off laptop. Turn on the laptop and try to enter the BIOS. Common keys to enter BIOS are F2, F10, Delete, or Esc (there should be an options list displayed while the laptop is at the start of turning). Once you are in BIOS, (or, if you didn't get into BIOS but the laptop booted from the flash drive you can ignore this part) go to Boot Options and look for something similar to Boot Priority list. Once you find it, move the USB option to the top of the list (it might list USB drive, USB storage, USB HDD, or the actual USB you have plugged in; you are not looking for USB CD/DVD Drive, or USB Ethernet). Exit BIOS, saving changes.

The laptop should now reboot and then boot from the flash drive. Once it has booted, you will be given the option to Install or Try the OS. I suggest you select Try & make sure that everything works smoothly. On an older laptop, it is likely that the Wifi will not work, but if you plug into Ethernet, you might be able to install a Wifi driver (open the Drivers utility & then wait for results).* Once you are satisfied that the distro will work with your hardware, go to the desktop and open the Install utility. It will guide you through the installation process. Default options are usually what you want. It will most likely offer to install along-side Windows 7; if you are done with Windows on the computer, select the option to install over 7 and have only Linux (THIS OPTION WILL ERASE ANY & ALL DATA YOU HAD ON THE COMPUTER. MAKE SURE YOU DON'T WANT ANYTHING ON WINDOWS BEFORE CHOOSING THIS OPTION).

If you have any issues, feel free to PM me for help.

*If you install a driver before installing, you will probably have to install the driver again after you have installed the OS. Also, if you see an option for installing a Raedon graphics driver, it is probably a good idea not to unless you have display issues. The open-source driver is considered safer (the proprietary driver can cause overheating issues).

Step by Step guide:

  1. Back up your computer with a backup program - Guide - This will allow you to have a full backup of windows, if you later on decide to backpedal.

  2. Pick a Linux Distro - Overview at Distrowatch - I would recommend Linux Mint or Ubuntu, since mostly it will probably just work and feel familiar. You can also go on askubuntu, search for issues there before asking for help.

  3. Download the ISO file for your distro (check Mint link above). Use Unetbootin to make a bootable USB stick or burn the ISO to a CD, either will work.

  4. Create an empty hard drive partition with as much space, as you want to give Linux (should be at least 4 gigs, give it as much as you can), if you want to dual boot. Do not format it.

  5. Start your PC in BIOS to change the boot order on your PC to boot from USB/CD and not go straight to windows on startup. Also turn off Secure Boot (enable it again after installing).

  6. Hardest part is over now. Shut down your PC, stick in the bootable USB or disk. Now you will boot into a "live session" of the distro of your choice, it's like a demo where you can try it out without installing anything yet. Click install, if you wish to do so. Follow this guide (for Mint) to walk you through the install process. Restart, you will boot into windows, no worries. Go back into your BIOS and put GRUB to the top of your boot order. Restart.

  7. Enjoy your new OS! Join the forums or IRC channels of the distro of your choice, if you want to learn more. Tip: Use the software manager in your distro to install new software, it's like an App Store, makes it easy for you.

Bonus: Download and use Gparted live session to delete windows and reorganize your partitions. Look up "things to do after installing Linux", for example you can install WINE to run windows Software. Learn to use the terminal. Go on Arch Wiki to learn more in depth about Linux stuff.
